Doctors Long Working Hours

By: Michael Duffett | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Summary:
The safer working hours campaign gained momentum last month following the tragic death of two woman in car accident. The driver in one vehicle was a doctor who had just come off a 28 hour stint, lost control of her car. It was thought she fell asleep at the wheel of her car. The narrative of this story surrounds this crash. We hear from junior doctors who have worked 35 hours in a row with no sleep. It seems to be madness. We speak to an expert on sleep deprivation and its effect on the mind and body. We ask the department of health what is the reason for 30 hour stints and in light of the recent accident if they are planning to make any changes.

Press Release:


Doctors Drunk on Fatigue
Studies have shown that a 24-hour bout of sleep deprivation is equivalent to being intoxicated with alcohol. So, where does this leave medical interns and junior doctors? They are forced to work shifts of 30 hours or more—akin to four working days in a row—often without breaks and therefore likely to make mistakes while treating patients? Carte Blanche asks: when will doctors’ calls for safer working hours be heard?


Script:


The present HPCSA controversial regulations allows for 30 hours shifts for young junior intern doctors
We met with a junior doctor; lets call her Sarah, who had just competed a 35-hour shift, with no sleep.

Sarah: You almost feel like you are a zombie, like you are floating on air.

Errors start creeping in.

Sarah: Just last night I made the mistake of writing 50mg of morphine instead of 5.

Fortunately she realized her mistake before any harm was done, but such mishaps don’t surprise Dr Irshaad ebrahim who head up a sleep clinic.

Dr Ebrahim: 24 hours of sleep deprivation is equivalent to being intoxicated with alcohol.

LINK: But even common sense dictates that 30 hours of uninterrupted work will have a significant mental and physical impact. We've spoken to other doctors who say that they often work far longer than that, many times without a single break.

On the 3rd of June, a young intern Ilne Markwat finished a 28-hour stint at Paarl Hospital in the Cape and headed home.

LINK: Ilne was travelling from paarl in the direction of Cape Town on this highway when a little way up the road she lost control and veered into oncoming traffic.

Her car went through the barriers and crashed head on in to bakkie carrying Carol Mostert and driven by her fiancé Johannes Pretorious.

Johannes: I can’t even remember the impact. I know I, when I regained my conscious I saw carol's head was down like this and I saw the blood.

Carol Mostert’s sister heard about the accident and rushed to the scene. emergency workers tried to hold her back.

Janine: I forced my way through and I just said to her that I am here before she went in.

Her sister Carol, Johan and Ilne and two others were rushed to hospital but Ilna died en route. Carol who was critically inured started to show signs of recovery and after 12 days was able to communicate with her injured finance Johan.

Johannes: We started our day even in hospital. We would say, " More my skat" then she would say "More my lief" Then when we go to sleep, "Nag my skat, Nag my lief" and then....

But she developed complications and her condition deteriorated rapidly.

Johannes: Monday I went to visit her again and the next week Monday she was gone.

Carol leaves three children behind. Media reports have suggested that Ilne may have fallen asleep behind the wheel of her car.

Janine: I don't blame ilne for this. I don't blame her for the death of my sister. She lost a life; she was 25 years old as well. It's unnecessary. It should have happened.

Sarah who studied with Ilne was shattered by her passing

Sarah: It’s not right, it’s not fair. The way that I have been able to come to peace with her death is that perhaps her death and the death of the passenger in the other car, perhaps their deaths are the catalyst to change.

And change is what the safe working hours campaign is demanding. The campaign started after 5th year medical students of the university of Stellenbosch completed an ethics assignment, which focused on international research on medical errors and doctor fatigue.

Helene: We saw that working hour regulations makes a massive impact on the quality of care that you offer to your patients.

One study they referenced was that when working shifts longer than 24 hours interns made 5 times more serious diagnostic errors.

Dr. Ebrahim: It's strange that the medical education community and the medical community at large hasn’t actually taken into account the scientific data that is there to apply to themselves.

Ironically Ilne was part of that ethics assignment and the campaign.

Helene: She was an incredibly kind doctor towards her patient so I think her death is a great loss to the South African population at large.

John: Without wanting to underemphasize the tragedy, the deaths of carol and ilne might well lead to some sort of change?

Helene: I think so. I think the Safe Working Hours campaign has built up a lot of momentum and we not going to stop until we see real changes on the ground in the hospitals.

Already 7000 signatures have been signed on an online petition urging the dept. of health to review doctors working hours. Dr Terrence Carter of the dept. of health says that he can’t comment on the cause of the accident till an investigation report has been completed. We asked him if he was aware of any other incidents caused by doctor fatigue.

Dr. Carter: The answer to your question is no. We have never been made aware of any instance where as a result of fatigue there has been either and incident with an intern or junior doctor or for that matter with a patient in terms of lack of judgment.

But posts from junior doctors on the safe working hours campaign claim to provide such examples. Junior doctors give examples of accidents they have been involved in as a result of exhausting shifts, of the stress they have suffered. One junior dr wrote – “eventually after a full month of sleep deprivation and constant psychological battering, I became suicidal and had to be hospitalized and put under psychiatric and psychological care”
And the mishaps. One intern wrote that he forgot to close an incubator door and a sick baby fell to the floor. Another mislabeled blood, another suffered a needle stuck injury and had to go onto arvs. Young doctors report that their cognitive and motor functions become affected by sleep deprivation.

Sarah: And that’s quite a problem at 3 o clock in the morning when you've lost depth perception to try and put a drip up on a ten day old baby and you end up poking that baby five or six times,

Junior doctors are required to work these 30-hour and longer shifts several times a month – that is equivalent to working 4 working days in a row with no or little sleep.

And this is unacceptable to also the junior doctors association of South Africa.

Dr Van Niekerk: I think there has been a misnomer or a notion that just because it is something that ahs been in place for so long that very senior doctors have been through that it should just be carried on. Clearly from doctor’s deaths up until mistakes up until occupational injuries and patient’s lives being put in danger, this is something that needs to change.

Dr. carter: I think that the increase in population, the increase in the burden of disease, the increase in the work load has led to a situation where doctors hardly get any rest when they work during the night.

It seems that pressure from Judasa and the safe working hours campaign is finally working. The dept. of health has set up a task team to review these long shifts.

Dr. carter: We expect the first recommendation to come out certainly within the next three months.

And that can’t come sooner for fatigued junior doctors.

Dr.. Van Niekerk: My passion for medicine is immense. There is nothing else that I would like to do from being a doctor but that within itself does not mean that we need to use doctors and work them into the ground because these are the same doctors who are now thinking about other options, of leaving the profession, of going some place else. Of going overseas because they feel that they are working to the limit on exhaustion.

Sarah: I honestly don’t know how we do it.

But somehow these interns are persevering.

Sarah: We just do because we have to and its not because there is some kind of penalty to it. It’s that we genuinely care about our patients and who is going to do it if I don’t?


PROMO 1
A tragic accident thought to have been caused by a fatigued doctor has propelled The safe working hours campaign into the spotlight. Their aim – to reduce the current 30 hour shifts.
Helene: We not going to stop until we see real change on the ground in the hospitals

PROMO 2
Junior doctors and interns often work 30 hours and longer shifts with no sleep.
Dr: 24 hours of sleep deprivation is equivalent to being completely intoxiacated with alcohol.
The safer hours working campaign is demanding change.

PROMO 3
The tragic deaths of a fatigued doctor and another woman in a car accident has propelled long doctors working hours into the spotlight.
